reasoning: This is a narrative review article synthesizing existing literature on schizophrenia's neurochemistry, circuits, symptoms and treatments. It does not involve the generation or use of any specific software tools, nor does it generate or analyze a new dataset. It is a qualitative synthesis of prior research findings without computational or data-driven methodology.

This is a consensus guideline document synthesizing existing literature and expert opinion to produce clinical recommendations. It does not involve development or use of software, nor does it generate or use a specific dataset in the research sense; it draws on prior systematic reviews and case reports as evidence sources but does not analyze a dataset itself.

The study uses existing software (TopoToolbox V2) to process a nationwide DEM, without modifying or extending the tool itself, so software is 'Used' rather than 'Generated'. However, the research generates a new national-scale geodatabase of catchment and stream network morphometric characteristics, which is a substantial new dataset created and shared (via an interactive ArcGIS web-app) as a core output of the research, making it Data Generated (D1).

The paper develops a visualization tool integrating Jaya algorithm with Latin Hypercube Sampling for graph drawing - this is new/extended software developed by the research team, playing a central role in achieving research goals (S1). For data, they generated synthetic graph datasets using the Erdős–Rényi model with varying nodes/edges specifically for their experiments, alongside using some real-world datasets. Since new synthetic data was generated as part of the research to test their algorithm, and generated data takes precedence per the notes, this falls under D1.

This is a study protocol for a future randomised clinical trial. No software is developed or used in a substantial research role (only mentions of standard online questionnaires for data collection, not a specific software tool), and no data has been generated or used yet since the trial has not been conducted - this is purely a protocol describing planned methodology.

The study generated new primary data through interviews with lead nurses/stakeholders and surveys of nurses/midwives across four cohorts (2019-22) to assess confidence and importance of genomics competencies. This survey and interview data is newly collected by the research team as part of the study, making it data generated (D1). There is no mention of any software being developed or used as a substantial part of the research methodology - the analysis appears to involve standard statistical scoring (Likert scale means) and thematic analysis of qualitative data, without reliance on specific software tools that play a substantial role in the research goals, so this falls under No Software (S3).

The paper appears to be an editorial/introductory piece for a special issue in Neural Computing & Applications, discussing machine learning and deep learning applications in finance, education, and healthcare. Without a detailed abstract or methodology section indicating specific software development or dataset creation/use, and given this is likely an editorial summarizing contributions rather than presenting original research with concrete software or data artifacts, it is classified as no substantial software or data role.

The study uses existing treatment planning/TCP modeling tools but does not describe development of new software; the modeling and TCP calculations rely on established methods (radiotherapy treatment planning systems, published TCP models) rather than newly created software, so software is not a substantial generated output. The study generates new patient-specific data: pre-treatment ADC maps converted into cellular density maps and TCP maps for a cohort of ten GBM patients, and new dose escalation plans (BTV, SIB doses) derived specifically for this research, which are original data central to the research goals. This new imaging-derived and dosimetric data was generated and analyzed as part of the study, fitting D1 (Data Generated), while the software used (planning systems, TCP calculation) appears to be existing tools without substantial new development, but since the paper does not explicitly detail development of new custom software, it falls under 'No Software' (S3) as the software's role, while present, isn't described as a novel contribution or shared artifact of the research.

The study generated new data by applying a multiplexed immunofluorescence workflow to patient tissue samples (NLPHL and THRLBCL cases) to characterize immune cell phenotypes - this constitutes newly generated research data central to the study's findings. For software, the paper uses existing multiplexed immunofluorescence imaging and analysis platforms/software (standard image analysis tools) to quantify cell phenotypes, rather than developing new software tools as part of the research. There is no indication of a novel software package being created and shared; instead, existing imaging/analysis technology is applied to generate the biological dataset.

The study collected new survey data from 384 startup directors/representatives using questionnaires (BRCS, MBI-GS, custom Covid-19 stress assessment), constituting newly generated data central to the research (D1). For analysis, they used a GMDH neural network approach, which is an existing, established modeling technique/method rather than a newly developed software tool by the authors; there's no indication of a novel software tool being released. Thus the neural network software is used as an existing method (S2), while the data collected via surveys is generated by the researchers (D1).

The study generates new experimental data: an original X-ray crystal structure of AMG-176 bound to Mcl-1, plus new NMR-based conformer analysis data for the clinical inhibitors. These are novel datasets produced by the research team and are central to the paper's conclusions (likely deposited in the PDB), fitting D1. For software, the authors use standard existing crystallography and NMR data processing/analysis software (e.g., structure refinement, NMR analysis tools) to generate and interpret these structures, but they do not report developing or extending new software tools as part of this research - it's used as a means to an end. This fits S2 (Software Used).

This is a cluster randomized controlled trial that generated new primary data through repeated assessments of mothers and children (pregnancy, 3, 6, 15, 24 months) across 8 clinics. This data collection is central to the research goals and constitutes newly generated data (D1). There is no mention of any software tool being developed or substantially used as part of the research methodology - standard statistical analysis for RCTs was used, which does not rise to the level of a substantial software contribution (S3).

The researchers developed harmonised symptom/blood test phenotypes (code lists) applied to existing EHR data (UK Biobank and CPRD Gold linked to cancer registry data). These phenotypes represent newly generated data artifacts (coded symptom definitions) that are a core research output and are described as potentially useful for other researchers, indicating data generation (D1). No new software tool is developed or shared; standard statistical analysis (Poisson regression) was used, which does not constitute substantial software development, so S3 applies.

This is a perspective/opinion piece on decolonising the psychology curriculum. It does not involve any software development or use, nor does it generate, collect, or analyze empirical data. It is a conceptual/argumentative discussion drawing on existing literature and recommendations, without a dataset or software tool being central to the research.

The paper's primary contribution is compiling and sharing a novel global dataset (DOCU-CLIM) of 621 documentary climate time series, including both published and previously unpublished records, which is itself a research goal and is shared as a dataset. This clearly represents new/generated data (D1). While the authors perform statistical evaluations (correlations, proxy forward models) to validate the series, there is no mention of developing or substantially extending any software tool; standard analysis techniques are used without the software itself being a research product or focus. Hence, software is not a substantial or generated component of this paper's contribution, categorizing it as S3.

The study generated new sediment core metabarcoding data (community-level functional biodiversity measurements spanning 100 years) as a primary research output, which constitutes newly generated data central to the research goals. Additionally, they developed a novel "conceptual framework" employing "explainable network models with multimodal learning" - a new AI/ML modeling approach/software framework specifically built for this multimodal biodiversity-environment correlation analysis, going beyond simply applying existing off-the-shelf tools. This represents substantial software development (S1) tailored to their explainable network architecture, combined with newly generated multilocus metabarcoding sediment data (D1) that is a core research product of the study.

This is a narrative/state-of-the-art review article summarizing existing literature on imaging techniques for blood-brain barrier dysfunction. It does not generate or use any specific software tool as part of a research methodology, nor does it generate or analyze a new dataset. It is a synthesis of existing knowledge for clinical guidance, so neither software nor data play a substantial role in producing new results.

This is a cross-sectional survey study where the researchers collected new primary data through a survey of 10,007 respondents in Malang, Indonesia, regarding COVID-19 knowledge, vaccine willingness, and uptake. This constitutes newly generated data as part of the research goals (D1). The analysis used standard statistical methods (linear regression, logistic regression, generalized structural equation modeling), which are standard statistical techniques rather than software that was developed or substantially extended by the research team; no specific custom software tool is described as being created or shared, so this falls under No Software (S3).

This is a review article discussing concepts and challenges in post-GWAS interpretation of AD and PD genetic risk loci. It does not report generation of new software or data, nor does it use a specific existing dataset or software tool as part of a research analysis—it synthesizes literature and discusses methodologies conceptually. Hence no substantial software or data role.

This is a narrative review article summarizing existing literature on MAIT cells and the microbiome. It does not generate or use any new software, nor does it generate or analyze new datasets; it synthesizes prior findings and speculates on future research directions.

The researchers developed a novel counterfactual GAN architecture specifically for this study, which is a substantial new software contribution central to the research goals (generating synthetic counterfactual OCT images and longitudinal series). This constitutes S1. The data used, however, is the existing UK Biobank OCT dataset (85,709 adults), which is a pre-existing large-scale population cohort not generated by the research team, making this D2 (Data Used).

The researchers used an existing pretrained language model (GPT-2) as a tool to generate simulated narratives, rather than developing new software themselves (though they provide a Python tutorial, this is more a demonstration/tutorial than novel research software). This constitutes 'Software Used' (S2). However, they generated new simulated narrative data (FTD-like text corpora) by perturbing model parameters, which is central to their research goals and appears to be shared/published as part of the study - this constitutes 'Data Generated' (D1).

This is a study protocol for a prospective cross-sectional survey. The researchers will use an existing commercial platform, Qualtrics XM, to design and disseminate the survey (software used, not developed by the team), which plays a substantial role in data collection. The survey itself will generate new primary data (responses from surgeons internationally about SSI prevention practices) that is a core research goal and will be collected and analyzed as part of this study. Since no new software is being developed by the research team, but new data will be generated through the survey, this fits S2D1.

This is a clinical pharmacology study (phase 1 crossover trials) generating new pharmacokinetic data (Cmax, AUC values) from healthy subjects to assess drug-drug interactions with rezafungin. No software tool development or use is described as central to the research; standard statistical analyses were performed but no specific software is highlighted as playing a substantial, novel role. The primary output is newly generated clinical trial data (PK parameters, adverse event data), making this D1. No mention of software generation or specific software packages central to achieving results, so S3.

The study uses existing UK Biobank data (anthropometric, physical activity, dietary and FFQ data) to operationalise a pre-existing standardized scoring system (2018 WCRF/AICR Score). No new software tool is developed or shared; standard statistical calculations are performed. The data used is existing UK Biobank data, not newly generated by the research team, thus classified as Data Used (D2) and No Software (S3).

This is a literature review paper discussing existing cardiovascular risk assessment methods, biomarkers, and ocular imaging concepts. It does not generate or use any specific software tool, nor does it generate or analyze a specific dataset. It's a narrative/synthesis review without empirical data collection or software development/use.

The study uses Google Trends (existing tool/data source) and Joinpoint regression software (existing NIH tool) to analyze pre-existing Google search data. No new software was developed, and the data (Google search trends) is existing publicly available data used for analysis rather than newly generated by the researchers.

This is a qualitative interview study collecting new primary data (in-depth interviews with DOs and DMs) via Zoom, analyzed manually through thematic analysis - this constitutes newly generated data central to the research goals. No specialized software was developed or used substantially (analysis was manual thematic coding), so software plays no substantial role, placing it in S3. The new interview/qualitative data generated qualifies as D1.

This is a systematic review and meta-analysis that synthesizes existing published studies and national survey data on adolescent nutrition in Ethiopia. The researchers used existing data (from 76 articles and 2 national surveys) to calculate pooled prevalence estimates via meta-analysis, but did not generate new primary data themselves - they used existing published data. No new software was developed; standard statistical/meta-analysis tools were likely used for pooling estimates, but software is not a focus or substantial contribution of the research, and no specific software tool is mentioned as being developed or extended. The paper is primarily about synthesizing existing literature data rather than generating new data or software.

The study generated new experimental data by recording high-density surface EMG from 18 children (9 TD, 9 DCD) during handgrip contractions, which was decomposed into motor unit firing data - this is newly generated data central to the research goals (D1). For software, the study used existing EMG decomposition algorithms/software (e.g., standard motor unit decomposition tools typically used in HDsEMG research) to process the recorded signals, but there is no indication that the research team developed or substantially extended new software as part of this study - they used established decomposition and analysis methods (S2).
